This means that chat participants may see deviating orders of messages, replies to messages they don't even see. In theory, it's even possible that several messages from the same sender arrive and are displayed in wrong order.  Idea 1: Sort the conversation view by "sent" timestamp. See also Display send date for incoming messages #806. Problem: What is the "sent" date? Is it reliable? Is it set by the client or the TS server (farm)? Idea 2: Give each message a sequence number generated by the TextSecure server. Sort conversation view according to those numbers. Problem: Many, but not all messages go through the TS server. Idea 3: Employ vector clocks.

<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>, the App must sort the "conversation view" by "sent" time.
<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>, the App must display the "messages" in the "conversation view" in the same order for all "chat participants".

requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 7345 | Request Title - Better Media Saving Behavior | Request Description - I have:   searched open and closed issues for duplicates  read https://github.com/WhisperSystems/Signal-Android/wiki/Submitting-useful-bug-reports  Bug description. One of the features that was missing for a long time but thankfully has been recently implemented was the ability to swipe through the images without having to keep going back to the index and always having it start at the top. Kudos and thanks for that. However, another element exists that can be greatly improved and probably just got missed; and hopefully can be added. Currently each picture ("media") provides you the save button on the top. However, it never detects that the item has already been saved and you have to just remember it or go check your on device gallery to see if it is already there. Instead, it simply keeps making duplicates of the item and just incrementing it. It would't be too difficult to do a simple if/exists > show view/share icon else/doesn't > show save icon (as it is now). This will spare the need to save multiple duplicates and incrementing it when you can simply provide a visual check that it has already been saved. It is simply better UX and cleaner that way. Steps to reproduce.  save an item save it again you have a duplicate with a -1 at the end save it again you now have 3 with a -1 and -2 of the same item repeat and goes on as long as you keep saving Expected result: Detect that the item has already been saved and either provide a view icon or share icon to visually indicate it has been saved already, otherwise show the save button. A simple file system check for the item will facilitate this. Thanks in advance.

<MISSING_SCOPE>, if a picture has already been saved, then the App must show a view or share icon instead of the save button.
<MISSING_SCOPE>, if the user has already saved a "media item", then the App must show a "view" or "share" icon instead of the "save" button.
requirements.llm_rimay: For each picture, if the picture has already been saved to the device, then the Signal-Android application shall show the "view icon or share icon" instead of the "save button".

verdict.text:
On missing-slot detection, Track 1 is measurable here, but only for two slots. Scope (34 gold-missing) and condition (21) have real support. Actor and modalVerb have one gold-missing case each, and action has four. Their recall of 1.0 or 0.75 is anecdote, not evidence. On the slots that count, zsl does badly: it flagged 6 of 34 missing scopes and 6 of 21 missing conditions. Taken at face value, that means it fills scope and condition most of the time when the source never stated them.

Some of these fills are real fabrication. 592-Signal gets "For all the requests", 828-Signal gets "For all the TextSecure groups", and 757-Signal gets "For group chats". None of these scopes is in the source.

Others look like a scoring artefact. 107-Mastodon and 4333-Signal contain no scope or condition text at all, yet llm_slots records both as "filled". The parser seems to treat the absence of an explicit `<MISSING_SCOPE>` tag as a fill. The 28 "silent" scope fills are therefore an upper bound, and the true fabrication rate cannot be read off this run until that is checked.

The second pattern is an inversion of the human convention. Annotators treat "the App must" as the implied default actor and modal. zsl instead emits `<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB>`, which accounts for the 14 actor and 15 modalVerb false positives, for example 828-Signal, 937-Signal and 1363-Signal. The model is cautious exactly where the gold standard allows inference, and permissive where the gold expects a flag. This mismatch drives most of the 16 cases where the LLM called a requirement incomplete and the gold called it complete. It reads more like a prompt-specification gap than a judgement failure.

Conversion similarity sits clearly below the human-human ceiling on every metric. The gap is roughly 0.13 on seq_ratio, 0.13 on Jaccard and 0.08 on cosine. With 35 requirements, the gap is probably real, but the ceiling is inflated. All three annotators share the boilerplate prefix "<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>, the App must", and zsl's outputs systematically lack it. Much of the shortfall is therefore surface template divergence rather than worse requirement content. In 757-Signal and 828-Signal, the action wording is close to the humans' phrasing.

The Paska results mostly reflect the placeholder problem rather than independent quality problems. "Not requirement" (16 cases) and "Incomplete requirement" (8) fire on sentences where the actor and modal are placeholders, so Paska finds no system response. The split confirms this: pass rate is 0.75 when the LLM produced a complete sentence and 0.16 when it did not. The genuinely content-level smells are single instances: a vague verb in 7310-Signal and condition-after-response ordering in 175-Signal.

Two outputs touch atomicity even though this set was filtered to atomic requirements. Paska flags 6457-Signal as non-atomic, and the LLM itself tagged 937-Signal `<NON_ATOMIC>`. That is worth a manual look, but two cases support no conclusion.

The sample is small and mostly Signal requests. This is one zsl run with no comparison strategy, and it covers only the easier atomic subset, so none of this generalises to unfiltered requirements.

The most useful next step is to fix the measurement before comparing strategies:

1. Audit how llm_slots marks scope and condition as "filled" when no text is present.
2. Revise the prompt so the model always writes explicit `<MISSING_SCOPE>`/`<MISSING_CONDITION>` tags and uses "the App" as the default actor, matching the annotation guideline.
3. Rerun zsl, then fsl and cot, against the corrected scorer.

Until then, Track 1 numbers for scope and Paska pass rates mix model behaviour with format and parser effects.
